title: Difference between ASP.NET and ASP.NET Core
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between ASP.NET (Framework) and ASP.NET Core?

story.setup: Imagine two office buildings owned by the same company: an old landmark tower built in the 1990s, and a brand-new modular building built from scratch.
scenes: The old tower (ASP.NET Framework) only has an address on Windows Street — it was built with Windows-only foundations, and it will never move.
The new building (ASP.NET Core) is modular and can be assembled anywhere — Windows, Linux, a shipping container (Docker) — because it doesn't depend on one city's infrastructure.

In the old tower, every department (DI, config) hires outside contractors (Unity, Ninject) because the building has no built-in facilities. The new building has its own in-house services team (built-in DI) from day one.

The old tower starts its business day by reading a giant printed policy binder (web.config XML) and ringing a bell at Application_Start (Global.asax). The new building just runs a lightweight startup script (Program.cs) that assembles a pipeline of checkpoints (middleware).
When the company needs two versions of the same building running side-by-side for different clients, only the new modular building supports it — the old tower is a single fixed structure.
story.moral: ASP.NET Core isn't a renovation of ASP.NET — it's a ground-up rewrite optimized for speed, portability, and modern DevOps, while the old ASP.NET Framework stays frozen on Windows/IIS.

analogy: ASP.NET is a landmark building fixed to one city (Windows/IIS); ASP.NET Core is a modular building you can assemble anywhere.
explanation: ASP.NET (Framework 4.x) is Windows-only, hosted exclusively on IIS, closed-source in its core runtime, and configured via XML in web.config with application lifecycle events wired through Global.asax. ASP.NET Core is a complete rewrite: cross-platform (Windows/Linux/macOS), hostable on Kestrel, IIS, Nginx, or inside Docker containers, fully open source, and significantly faster due to a leaner, modular runtime. It has dependency injection built into the framework instead of relying on third-party containers like Unity or Ninject, uses appsettings.json plus environment variables for configuration, and replaces Global.asax with Program.cs and an explicit middleware pipeline. MVC and Web API, which were two separate frameworks in classic ASP.NET, are unified into a single framework in Core. Core also supports side-by-side versioning, so multiple applications on the same machine can target different .NET versions independently.
interviewAnswerShort: ASP.NET Core is a complete, cross-platform rewrite of ASP.NET — open source, faster, with built-in DI and a middleware pipeline replacing web.config, HTTP modules, and Global.asax.
interviewAnswerDetailed: ASP.NET Framework is Windows-only and tied to IIS, while ASP.NET Core runs cross-platform on Kestrel, IIS, Nginx, or Docker. Core is open source and built with performance as a first-class goal, so it consistently benchmarks faster than Framework. Dependency injection is built into Core's runtime rather than requiring a third-party container. Configuration moved from XML-based web.config to appsettings.json plus environment variables, which plays much better with containers and cloud deployments. Startup logic moved from Global.asax event handlers to Program.cs, where you explicitly compose a middleware pipeline instead of relying on implicit HTTP modules and handlers. MVC and Web API, which were separate frameworks with separate base classes in classic ASP.NET, are unified into one framework in Core. Finally, Core supports side-by-side installation of multiple versions, so you're not forced to upgrade every app on a machine at once.

codeExample.explanation: Program.cs replaces Global.asax and web.config — DI registration and the middleware pipeline are both explicit, readable C# code instead of XML and hidden event hooks.

mistakes: Assuming ASP.NET Core is just a new version of ASP.NET rather than a full rewrite with a different runtime model.
Trying to host ASP.NET Core exclusively on IIS and not knowing Kestrel is the actual cross-platform web server.
Forgetting that MVC and Web API were separate frameworks (System.Web.Mvc vs System.Web.Http) in classic ASP.NET but are unified in Core.
Not knowing Global.asax's role, so being unable to answer what replaced it and why.
Assuming you must use a third-party DI container in Core when one is built in.

followUps.question: What was Global.asax used for?
followUps.answer: It held application-level event handlers in classic ASP.NET: Application_Start (register routes/filters/bundles, runs once at startup), Session_Start, Application_Error (catches any unhandled exception app-wide), and Application_End. In ASP.NET Core, Program.cs and the middleware pipeline take over this responsibility explicitly.

followUps.question: Can you run ASP.NET Core on IIS at all?
followUps.answer: Yes — IIS can act as a reverse proxy in front of Kestrel (the ASP.NET Core Module forwards requests to Kestrel), or you can use IIS in-process hosting. But Kestrel itself is the cross-platform server; IIS is now optional, not mandatory.

followUps.question: Why is ASP.NET Core generally faster than ASP.NET Framework?
followUps.answer: It has a leaner, modular request pipeline with no legacy HTTP modules/handlers overhead, a more efficient Kestrel server, ahead-of-time and tiered JIT compilation improvements in the .NET runtime, and you only pull in the NuGet packages/middleware you actually need instead of a large fixed framework.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Old tower vs modular building — same company, totally different construction.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture yourself walking out of a locked Windows-only skyscraper (ASP.NET) into an open-air modular building that you can bolt together on any street (Core) — Kestrel is the crew that assembles it anywhere.

bestPractices: For new projects, always start with ASP.NET Core unless a hard legacy dependency forces classic ASP.NET.
Use appsettings.{Environment}.json plus environment variables for configuration instead of web.config-style hardcoding.
Plan Framework-to-Core migrations incrementally (strangler-fig pattern) rather than a big-bang rewrite.
Leverage built-in DI rather than bolting on a third-party container unless you need advanced features it lacks.
performanceTips: Kestrel alone is very fast, but for public-facing apps still put it behind a reverse proxy (IIS, Nginx, or a cloud load balancer) for things like TLS termination and process management.
Trim middleware to only what each app needs — every registered middleware adds a small per-request cost.

quiz.question: Which of these is TRUE about ASP.NET Core compared to classic ASP.NET?
options: It has dependency injection built in
It uses web.config for all configuration
It merges routing but keeps MVC and Web API as separate frameworks
quiz.explanation: ASP.NET Core ships with a built-in DI container, unlike classic ASP.NET which relies on third-party libraries like Unity or Ninject.

quiz.question: What replaced Global.asax's Application_Start in ASP.NET Core?
quiz.explanation: ASP.NET Core moves application startup logic into Program.cs, where services are registered and the middleware pipeline is explicitly configured.

flashcards.front: Is ASP.NET Core cross-platform?
flashcards.back: Yes — Windows, Linux, macOS, via Kestrel.

flashcards.front: What replaced web.config for configuration?
flashcards.back: appsettings.json plus environment variables.

flashcards.front: What replaced Global.asax?
flashcards.back: Program.cs plus the middleware pipeline.

flashcards.front: Is DI built into ASP.NET Core?
flashcards.back: Yes, natively — no third-party container required.

revision30: ASP.NET Core is a complete rewrite of ASP.NET: cross-platform, open source, faster, with built-in DI, appsettings.json config, and Program.cs/middleware replacing web.config and Global.asax.
revision2min: Classic ASP.NET Framework is Windows-only, hosted solely on IIS, closed-source at its core, and configured through web.config XML with lifecycle events in Global.asax. It relies on third-party DI containers like Unity or Ninject, and MVC/Web API exist as two separate frameworks. ASP.NET Core rewrites all of this: it's cross-platform and can run on Kestrel, IIS, Nginx, or Docker; it's open source; it's significantly faster due to a leaner pipeline; dependency injection is built in; configuration uses appsettings.json plus environment variables, which fits containers and cloud deployment far better; and startup/middleware is explicit C# code in Program.cs rather than implicit event hooks. MVC and Web API are unified into one framework, and Core supports side-by-side versioning so different apps on one machine can target different .NET versions.
challenge: You're asked to migrate a large classic ASP.NET MVC 5 app to ASP.NET Core without downtime. Outline your migration strategy and name at least two APIs or patterns that won't have a direct 1:1 equivalent.
summary: ASP.NET Core is a ground-up, cross-platform rewrite of ASP.NET Framework — faster, open source, with built-in DI and an explicit middleware pipeline replacing web.config and Global.asax.

title: What is Middleware? Build a custom one.
interviewQuestion: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core, and how would you write a custom middleware component?

story.setup: Picture an international airport. Every passenger (HTTP request) must pass through a sequence of checkpoints before reaching the gate (your controller).
scenes: First is the emergency response station (Exception middleware) — it wraps the entire journey, ready to catch any crisis anywhere down the line.
Next, passengers with only a boarding pass to the duty-free shop (Static Files) get waved through a fast lane — no need for a passport check to buy chocolate.
Then comes the signage system (Routing) that decides which gate a passenger is even headed to, before anyone checks their identity for that gate.
Only now does passport control (Authentication) check WHO you are, followed by a boarding-pass class check (Authorization) confirming WHAT you're allowed to board.

Finally the passenger reaches the gate agent (the Controller/endpoint). If passport control ran before signage, the agent wouldn't even know which gate's rules to enforce — that's why order matters, and any checkpoint can pull a passenger aside and send them straight back (short-circuit) without ever reaching the gate.
story.moral: Middleware is an ordered sequence of checkpoints — each one can inspect, modify, pass along via next(), or stop the request cold, and the order they're registered in determines what each checkpoint is allowed to know.

analogy: Middleware is airport security — each checkpoint (static files, routing, authentication, authorization) can inspect you, wave you through, or turn you back before you ever reach the gate.
explanation: Middleware components are objects that form a pipeline: every incoming request passes through them in registration order, and the response passes back through them in reverse order. Each middleware receives the HttpContext and a reference to the next delegate in the pipeline; it can inspect or modify the request, call await _next(context) to pass control forward, or short-circuit by not calling next and writing a response directly. A custom middleware class needs a constructor that accepts RequestDelegate next (plus any singleton services via DI) and a public InvokeAsync (or Invoke) method that takes HttpContext. It's typically registered via an app.UseMiddleware<T>() extension method wrapped in a clean UseXxx() call. Order is critical: exception handling must wrap everything so it's registered first, static files should be early to avoid paying auth costs for assets, routing must run before authentication/authorization so endpoint metadata like [Authorize] is known, and authentication must run before authorization so an identity exists to check permissions against.
interviewAnswerShort: Middleware are ordered pipeline components that each get the request, can act on it, call next() to pass it along, or short-circuit and return a response — order of registration is critical because each component only sees what earlier ones passed through.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Middleware forms a chain: Request → [Exception] → [Static Files] → [Routing] → [AuthN] → [AuthZ] → Controller, and the response travels back up the same chain in reverse. Each middleware is a class with a RequestDelegate _next field injected via constructor, and an InvokeAsync(HttpContext context) method — inside it, you do work before calling await _next(context), and can do more work after that call runs and returns, which is how you can measure things like request timing. If a middleware doesn't call next, it short-circuits the pipeline entirely — nothing downstream runs. You register custom middleware either inline with app.Use(...) or as a class via an extension method that calls app.UseMiddleware<T>(). Ordering rules that come up constantly: exception handling must be registered first so it wraps every other component; static files early, before auth, so serving a CSS file doesn't pay authentication overhead; routing before authentication/authorization, because AuthZ needs to know the matched endpoint's [Authorize] attributes, which routing determines; and authentication before authorization, because you can't check permissions for an identity you haven't established yet.

codeExample.explanation: A custom middleware measures request duration around await _next(context); the correct pipeline order ensures exception handling wraps everything and authentication precedes authorization.

mistakes: Registering [Authorize]-checking middleware (UseAuthorization) before UseAuthentication, so no identity exists yet to authorize.
Placing UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization before UseRouting, so endpoint metadata like [Authorize] attributes isn't known yet.
Registering the global exception handler last instead of first, so it sits inside everything and misses errors thrown by earlier middleware.
Putting UseStaticFiles after authentication, forcing every image/CSS/JS request to pay the authentication cost.
Forgetting to call await _next(context) when it should be called, silently short-circuiting the pipeline.

followUps.question: Why does middleware order matter?
followUps.answer: Each middleware only sees what earlier middleware passed to it, and any middleware can short-circuit everything after it. If routing hasn't run yet, authorization doesn't know which endpoint's [Authorize] rules apply; if exception handling isn't first, it can't catch errors thrown earlier in the pipeline.

followUps.question: When would you write custom middleware versus using a filter?
followUps.answer: Write middleware when a concern applies to every request regardless of controller — correlation IDs for tracing, global exception handling, tenant resolution in multi-tenant apps, request/response logging, rate limiting, or maintenance-mode 503s. The rule of thumb: cross-cutting concern at the HTTP level → middleware; needs MVC context like the action or ModelState → filter; already built in (e.g. UseRateLimiter) → just use the built-in.

followUps.question: What's the difference between Use, Run, and Map?
followUps.answer: Use can call next() and continue the pipeline. Run is terminal — it never calls next and always ends the pipeline there. Map branches the pipeline based on a path prefix, routing a subset of requests into a separate sub-pipeline.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Passport control before boarding-pass check — auth before authz, always.
memoryHack.mnemonic: ESRA-AA: Exception, Static, Routing, AuthN, AuthZ.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Walk through the airport terminal in order: emergency exits (exception) wrap the whole building, duty-free fast lane (static files), the signage board (routing) telling you which gate, passport control (authN), then the gate agent checking your ticket class (authZ) — reversing any two breaks the whole terminal's logic.

bestPractices: Always register exception-handling middleware first so it wraps the entire pipeline.
Keep middleware focused on one cross-cutting concern per class for testability and reuse.
Expose custom middleware via a UseXxx() extension method for clean, readable Program.cs registration.
Use Map/MapWhen to branch the pipeline for distinct sub-apps (e.g. health checks) instead of littering conditionals inside one middleware.
performanceTips: Order matters for performance too — put cheap, high-rejection-rate checks (like static file serving or rate limiting) early so expensive downstream work is avoided.
Avoid heavy synchronous work inside middleware; always await async calls to not block Kestrel's thread pool.

quiz.question: What must a custom middleware class's request-handling method be named?
quiz.explanation: ASP.NET Core's middleware convention requires a public Invoke or InvokeAsync method accepting HttpContext.

quiz.question: Which middleware ordering is correct?
quiz.explanation: Routing must resolve the endpoint (and its [Authorize] metadata) before authentication establishes identity, which must happen before authorization checks permissions.

flashcards.front: What does calling next() in middleware do?
flashcards.back: Passes control to the next middleware in the pipeline; skipping it short-circuits the request.

flashcards.front: Use vs Run vs Map?
flashcards.back: Use continues the pipeline; Run is terminal; Map branches by path prefix.

flashcards.front: Why register exception middleware first?
flashcards.back: So it wraps every other middleware and can catch errors thrown anywhere downstream.

flashcards.front: Why must routing run before authorization?
flashcards.back: Authorization needs the matched endpoint's [Authorize] metadata, which routing determines.

revision30: Middleware is an ordered pipeline where each component can act, call next() to continue, or short-circuit. Order matters: exception handling first, static files early, routing before auth, authentication before authorization.
revision2min: Middleware components form a request pipeline: requests flow through in registration order, responses flow back in reverse. Each middleware gets HttpContext and a RequestDelegate next; it can inspect/modify the request, call await _next(context) to continue, or short-circuit by writing a response directly without calling next. Custom middleware is a class with a constructor taking RequestDelegate next plus DI services, and an InvokeAsync(HttpContext) method, typically exposed via a UseXxx() extension method. The canonical order is: exception handler first (wraps everything), HTTPS redirection, static files early (avoid auth cost on assets), routing (determines the endpoint), CORS, authentication (who you are), authorization (what you can do), then endpoint execution. Getting this order wrong is a classic bug: AuthZ before AuthN means no identity exists to check; Auth before Routing means [Authorize] metadata isn't known yet; exception handler last means it can't catch earlier errors. Use vs Run vs Map: Use can continue the chain, Run is terminal, Map branches the pipeline by path.
challenge: Write a custom middleware that adds a correlation ID (a GUID) to every request if one isn't already present in an X-Correlation-Id header, attaches it to the logging scope, and includes it in the response headers — and explain exactly where in the pipeline you'd register it and why.
summary: Middleware is an ordered, composable pipeline of request/response handlers where registration order determines what each component can see and short-circuit.

title: What is Dependency Injection and its uses?
interviewQuestion: What is Dependency Injection, what are its uses, and how do you choose between Transient, Scoped, and Singleton?

story.setup: A restaurant kitchen doesn't grow its own vegetables or bottle its own water — ingredients are delivered to the chef, ready to use.
scenes: The chef (OrderService) doesn't personally drive to a farm to grow tomatoes; a supplier hands ingredients (IEmailService) directly to the kitchen through the delivery window (constructor). This is Dependency Injection — the class receives what it needs instead of creating it.
Disposable napkins (Transient services) are grabbed fresh for every single table — cheap, stateless, no need to reuse.
A table's shared serving platter (Scoped service) is used for the whole duration of one table's meal (one HTTP request) and then cleared away — never shared between two different tables at once.

The restaurant's single walk-in freezer (Singleton service) is shared by the entire kitchen for the whole night — expensive to build, so there's only ever one, and it must be safe for every chef to use concurrently.

A new chef made the mistake of storing today's specials board (a Scoped DbContext) inside the walk-in freezer (a Singleton) — now every table for the rest of the night sees stale, shared, conflicting specials. That's a captive dependency, and it breaks the kitchen.
story.moral: DI hands each class its dependencies instead of letting it create them — and choosing the right lifetime (Transient/Scoped/Singleton) is what keeps shared state from leaking across requests.

analogy: Dependency Injection is a restaurant kitchen receiving ingredients through a supply window instead of growing its own — the class just declares what it needs via its constructor.
explanation: Dependency Injection is a pattern where a class receives its dependencies from the outside (typically via its constructor) rather than constructing them itself, decoupling the class from concrete implementations. ASP.NET Core has a built-in DI container configured in Program.cs via builder.Services, with three lifetimes: Transient creates a new instance every time it's requested, ideal for lightweight, stateless services; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request, ideal for anything tied to a unit of work like DbContext; and Singleton creates one instance for the entire application lifetime, ideal for expensive, thread-safe shared resources like caches or IHttpClientFactory. Its uses include loose coupling (code depends on interfaces, not concrete classes), easy unit testing via mocking those interfaces, swapping implementations through configuration without code changes, and centralized lifetime management instead of manual object creation scattered everywhere. A dangerous mistake is a 'captive dependency' — injecting a Scoped service (like DbContext) into a Singleton, which captures that Scoped instance for the application's entire lifetime, causing it to outlive its intended request and misbehave or throw concurrency errors.
interviewAnswerShort: Dependency Injection means a class receives its dependencies via its constructor instead of creating them itself, giving loose coupling, testability via mocks, and centralized lifetime management through Transient, Scoped, and Singleton registrations.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Instead of a class newing up its own dependencies, ASP.NET Core's built-in DI container constructs and injects them, usually through the constructor. You register services in Program.cs with builder.Services.AddTransient/AddScoped/AddSingleton, mapping an interface to an implementation. Transient services get a brand-new instance every single time they're resolved — good for cheap, stateless services. Scoped services get one instance per HTTP request — this is essential for DbContext, because EF Core's change tracking is per-unit-of-work, DbContext isn't thread-safe, and a longer-lived instance would leak memory as its change tracker accumulates entities. Singleton services get exactly one instance for the whole app's lifetime — good for expensive, thread-safe shared resources like a cache or IHttpClientFactory. The uses of DI beyond lifetime management are loose coupling (depend on abstractions, not concretions), easier unit testing (swap real implementations for mocks/stubs), and configuration-driven implementation swapping. The most common interview trap is the captive dependency: injecting a Scoped service into a Singleton captures it for the app's whole lifetime, so a captured DbContext eventually throws concurrency exceptions across unrelated requests — the fix is to inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a fresh scope manually when needed.

codeExample.explanation: OrderService declares IEmailService as a constructor dependency; the three AddXxx calls show the three lifetimes, and the scope factory pattern shows how a Singleton safely obtains a Scoped DbContext without capturing it.

mistakes: Registering DbContext as Singleton or Transient instead of Scoped, causing thread-safety exceptions or breaking the unit-of-work boundary.
Injecting a Scoped service directly into a Singleton's constructor, creating a captive dependency.
Using the service locator anti-pattern (resolving from IServiceProvider inside business logic) instead of constructor injection.
Registering the interface and implementation with mismatched lifetimes across different registrations, causing subtle bugs.
Overusing Singleton for convenience without checking thread-safety, leading to race conditions.

followUps.question: Transient vs Scoped vs Singleton — how do you choose?
followUps.answer: Transient for stateless, cheap services. Scoped for anything tied to one request, especially DbContext. Singleton for expensive, thread-safe shared things like caches, configuration, or IHttpClientFactory.

followUps.question: Which lifetime should DbContext use, and why?
followUps.answer: Scoped. Three reasons: change tracking is per-request, so one SaveChanges() commits the request as a single unit of work; DbContext isn't thread-safe, so a Singleton shared across concurrent requests throws 'A second operation was started on this context…'; and memory grows with every tracked entity, so a Singleton would leak. Transient would create multiple contexts per request, breaking the unit-of-work boundary and any shared transaction.

followUps.question: What is a captive dependency?
followUps.answer: Injecting a Scoped service into a Singleton — the scoped object gets captured for the application's entire lifetime, so a DbContext outlives its request and starts failing. The fix is to inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope manually: using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope(); var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

followUps.question: Constructor vs property vs method injection?
followUps.answer: Constructor injection is the default — it makes dependencies explicit and mandatory, so the object is never in an invalid state. Property injection is for genuinely optional dependencies. Method injection passes a dependency only to the single method that needs it.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Transient = napkin, Scoped = table's platter, Singleton = the kitchen's freezer.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Walk the restaurant floor: napkins (Transient) restocked at every table visit, a shared platter (Scoped) that lives only for one table's meal, and the one walk-in freezer (Singleton) the whole kitchen shares all night — never store a table's platter inside the freezer.

bestPractices: Always register DbContext as Scoped (AddDbContext does this by default).
Prefer constructor injection over property or method injection unless the dependency is genuinely optional.
Depend on interfaces/abstractions in constructors, never concrete classes, to preserve testability.
When a Singleton needs a Scoped resource, inject IServiceScopeFactory and create scopes explicitly rather than capturing the dependency.
performanceTips: Singleton services avoid repeated construction cost, so use them for expensive-to-build, thread-safe resources like HttpClient (via IHttpClientFactory) or in-memory caches.
Avoid excessive Transient registrations for expensive-to-construct objects — the constant re-instantiation adds up under load.

quiz.question: What lifetime should EF Core's DbContext normally be registered with?
quiz.explanation: DbContext must be Scoped — its change tracker is per-request, and it isn't thread-safe, so Singleton throws concurrency errors and Transient breaks the unit-of-work boundary.

quiz.question: What is a captive dependency?
options: A service with no registered interface
A Scoped service injected into and captured by a Singleton
A Transient service that never gets disposed
A circular dependency between two services
quiz.explanation: Injecting a Scoped dependency (like DbContext) into a Singleton captures it for the app's full lifetime, causing it to outlive its intended request scope.

flashcards.front: What lifetime creates a new instance every resolution?
flashcards.back: Transient.

flashcards.front: What lifetime is correct for DbContext?
flashcards.back: Scoped — one per HTTP request.

flashcards.front: What lifetime is correct for a shared in-memory cache?
flashcards.back: Singleton — one per application.

flashcards.front: How do you safely use a Scoped service inside a Singleton?
flashcards.back: Inject IServiceScopeFactory and call CreateScope() to resolve it manually.

revision30: DI hands dependencies to a class via its constructor instead of the class creating them. Transient = new every time, Scoped = one per request (DbContext), Singleton = one per app. Never let a Singleton capture a Scoped dependency.
revision2min: Dependency Injection means classes declare what they need (usually via constructor parameters) and the DI container supplies it, rather than the class instantiating dependencies itself. ASP.NET Core's built-in container is configured with builder.Services.AddTransient/AddScoped/AddSingleton in Program.cs. Transient services are created fresh on every resolution — good for cheap, stateless work. Scoped services get one instance per HTTP request, which is exactly why DbContext must be Scoped: its change tracker represents one unit of work, it's not thread-safe, and a longer lifetime would leak memory. Singleton services live for the entire application — good for expensive, thread-safe shared resources like caches or IHttpClientFactory. Beyond lifetime management, DI's real value is loose coupling (depend on interfaces), testability (swap real services for mocks), and configuration-driven implementation swapping. The classic trap is a captive dependency — injecting a Scoped service into a Singleton captures it for the app's whole life, so a captured DbContext eventually throws thread-safety or staleness errors; the fix is injecting IServiceScopeFactory and creating a scope on demand. Constructor injection is preferred over property/method injection because it makes dependencies explicit and mandatory.
challenge: A Singleton IReportCache needs to occasionally query the database via a Scoped DbContext to refresh its cache on a timer. Design the class so it never becomes a captive dependency, and explain what would go wrong if you just injected AppDbContext into its constructor.
summary: Dependency Injection decouples classes from their dependencies via constructor injection, and choosing the right lifetime — Transient, Scoped, or Singleton — is what prevents state from leaking across unrelated requests.

title: What is Routing?
interviewQuestion: What is routing in ASP.NET Core and how does it map URLs to controller actions?

story.setup: Think of Google Maps directing a delivery driver to the right house — it doesn't just find any street, it finds the exact address and the exact door.
scenes: Conventional routing is like a GPS with a general rule of thumb: 'go to whichever street matches {controller}, then the house numbered {action}, then optionally apartment {id}' — one flexible pattern covers many destinations.
Attribute routing is a hand-written address label pinned right on each building: [Route("api/[controller]")] on ProductsController literally stamps the building's street name onto the door.
A route constraint like {id:int} is a bouncer at the door checking that whatever number shows up is actually a number, not a name — /products/5 gets in, /products/abc doesn't match at all.

UseRouting() is the moment the GPS finishes calculating which exact address matches the incoming request; MapControllers() is the moment the driver actually knocks on that door and hands over the package — which is why authentication and authorization checkpoints sit between those two moments, once the address (and its rules) are known but before delivery happens.
story.moral: Routing is the map-matching engine that turns an incoming URL into a specific controller/action (and generates URLs back out) — and it must finish selecting the destination before authorization can decide who's allowed to receive the delivery.

analogy: Routing is Google Maps for your API — it matches an incoming URL to the exact controller/action 'address', with route constraints acting as the delivery bouncer checking id types along the way.
explanation: Routing maps an incoming request URL to the code that should handle it, and can also generate outbound URLs from route data. ASP.NET Core supports conventional routing, defined once with app.MapControllerRoute using a pattern like {controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}, typically used in traditional MVC apps, and attribute routing, where each controller or action is decorated with [Route] and [HttpGet]/[HttpPost] attributes, typically used in Web API controllers for precise, self-documenting URL definitions. Route parameters can carry constraints like {id:int}, {id:guid}, or {page:int:min(1)} to restrict what values match. In the pipeline, UseRouting() is the middleware that matches the incoming request to an endpoint (determining which controller/action and its metadata, like [Authorize] attributes), while MapControllers() (or the equivalent Map* calls) actually executes that matched endpoint — this is exactly why authentication and authorization middleware are registered between UseRouting() and MapControllers(), since AuthZ needs the endpoint's metadata resolved by routing but hasn't executed the endpoint yet.
interviewAnswerShort: Routing maps an incoming URL to the controller/action that handles it (and generates URLs back out), using either conventional patterns like {controller}/{action}/{id?} or attribute routing with [Route] and [HttpGet] on Web API controllers, with constraints like {id:int} restricting matches.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Routing is the mechanism that decides which piece of code handles an incoming HTTP request URL, and it can also build URLs back out from route values, which is how Url.Action or link generation works. Conventional routing, registered once via app.MapControllerRoute("default", "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}"), is typical for traditional server-rendered MVC apps where many controllers share one pattern. Attribute routing decorates controllers and actions directly, e.g. [Route("api/[controller]")] on a ProductsController combined with [HttpGet], [HttpGet("{id:int}")], giving explicit, self-documenting, and more flexible per-action URLs, which is standard for Web API controllers. Route constraints like {id:int}, {id:guid}, or {page:int:min(1)} restrict which values are allowed to match a segment, so a route only activates for correctly-typed input rather than failing inside the action. In the middleware pipeline, UseRouting() performs endpoint matching — deciding which endpoint a request maps to and exposing its metadata — while MapControllers() (or Map* endpoints generally) is where that matched endpoint actually executes. That's why authentication and authorization middleware sit between UseRouting() and MapControllers(): by the time AuthZ runs, routing has already determined the endpoint and any [Authorize] attributes on it, but the endpoint hasn't executed yet.

codeExample.explanation: Attribute routing on a Web API controller: [Route("api/[controller]")] sets the base path, and each action's own attribute (plus constraints like {id:int}) precisely defines its matching URL.

mistakes: Mixing conventional and attribute routing inconsistently, causing ambiguous route matches.
Forgetting route constraints (like {id:int}), letting non-numeric input reach the action and fail deep inside business logic instead of returning a clean 404.
Registering UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization before UseRouting, so endpoint metadata isn't resolved yet.
Assuming [ApiController] is optional decoration rather than what enables automatic model validation and other Web API conventions.
Not realizing MapControllers() must be called or no attribute-routed endpoints will ever be reachable.

followUps.question: What's the difference between UseRouting() and MapControllers()?
followUps.answer: UseRouting() performs endpoint matching — it decides which endpoint a request maps to and makes that endpoint's metadata (like [Authorize]) available to later middleware. MapControllers() is where that matched endpoint actually executes, which is why authentication/authorization sit in between.

followUps.question: Give an example of a route constraint and why you'd use one.
followUps.answer: {id:int} restricts a route segment to only match integers, so /products/5 matches but /products/abc doesn't match this route at all (and can 404 cleanly or fall through to another route) rather than reaching the action and failing during parsing.

followUps.question: When would you choose conventional routing over attribute routing?
followUps.answer: Conventional routing suits traditional server-rendered MVC apps with many similarly-shaped controller/action URLs sharing one pattern. Attribute routing suits Web APIs where each endpoint's URL, HTTP verb, and constraints need to be explicit and independently controlled.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Routing is Google Maps for your URLs — it finds the address before anyone checks your ID at the door.
memoryHack.mnemonic: R before A-A: Routing resolves the address before AuthN/AuthZ check the visitor.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a GPS calculating the destination address (UseRouting) before the delivery driver actually knocks (MapControllers) — the security guard (AuthZ) checks your badge only once the GPS has confirmed which door you're headed to.

bestPractices: Use attribute routing with [ApiController] for Web APIs to get explicit, self-documenting endpoint definitions.
Apply route constraints ({id:int}, {id:guid}) to fail fast on malformed input instead of letting it reach the action.
Keep route templates consistent and plural-noun-based across controllers for a predictable API surface.
Register UseRouting() before any middleware (auth, etc.) that depends on the matched endpoint's metadata.
performanceTips: Endpoint routing (the modern ASP.NET Core routing system) is optimized with a route table lookup, so having many routes has minimal per-request overhead compared to older regex-heavy routing.
Avoid overly generic catch-all routes that force the router to evaluate many candidates before matching.

Restricts the id segment to only match integer values
Converts id to a string automatically

options: Authorization needs the matched endpoint's metadata, which routing determines
It's just convention with no functional impact
UseAuthorization requires HTTPS which routing enables
Routing performs the actual authentication check
quiz.explanation: Authorization needs to inspect the matched endpoint's [Authorize] metadata, which only exists once UseRouting() has selected the endpoint.

title: What are Filters? What is an Action Filter?
interviewQuestion: What are filters in ASP.NET Core MVC, and what is an action filter specifically?

story.setup: Think of a TV studio's live broadcast pipeline, with distinct crew stations checking the show before and after the segment airs.
scenes: The security guard at the studio door (Authorization filter) checks credentials first, before anyone even walks toward the set.

The stage manager (Resource filter) does a quick prop check right after security but before the script (model binding) is even handed out — they can cancel the whole segment right there and cut to a rerun.

The floor director (Action filter) watches the segment live: OnActionExecuting shouts 'we're rolling' just before the host speaks, and OnActionExecuted shouts 'cut' right after, logging how the take went.
If a camera catches fire mid-segment (an unhandled exception), the emergency crew (Exception filter) is the only station that activates — it's not there for a normal broadcast.

After the segment airs, the broadcast engineer (Result filter) tweaks the final output — adding a lower-third caption — right before and after it's actually transmitted to viewers (the result executing).
story.moral: Filters are checkpoints inside the MVC pipeline, each specialized for a different stage and each with access to MVC-specific context (like ModelState) that raw middleware never sees.

analogy: Filters are TV studio crew stations inside the broadcast pipeline — authorization checks credentials at the door, action filters watch the live segment, and result filters tweak the output right before air.
explanation: Filters run at specific stages inside the ASP.NET Core MVC pipeline, for concerns that need action-level context that middleware doesn't have. There are five kinds: Authorization filters run first and back [Authorize]; Resource filters run after authorization but before model binding, useful for caching or short-circuiting; Action filters run immediately before and after the action method executes, via OnActionExecuting and OnActionExecuted, useful for logging, validation, and timing; Exception filters run only when an unhandled exception occurs, for centralized error handling; and Result filters run before and after the action's result executes, letting you modify the final response. An action filter is implemented by inheriting ActionFilterAttribute and overriding OnActionExecuting(ActionExecutingContext) to run code (and optionally set context.Result to short-circuit, e.g. on invalid ModelState) before the action runs, and OnActionExecuted(ActionExecutedContext) to run code after, including inspecting context.Exception. Filters can be applied to a single action, a whole controller, or registered globally via builder.Services.AddControllers(o => o.Filters.Add<T>()).
interviewAnswerShort: Filters are pipeline stages inside MVC — authorization, resource, action, exception, and result filters — that run at specific points around action execution and, unlike middleware, have access to MVC context like the action arguments and ModelState.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Filters let you inject logic at specific stages of the MVC request-processing pipeline, distinct from raw HTTP middleware because they run inside MVC and can see action-specific context. Authorization filters run first, backing attributes like [Authorize]. Resource filters run right after authorization but before model binding — useful for caching responses or short-circuiting expensive work early. Action filters wrap the actual action method call: OnActionExecuting runs immediately before the action, letting you inspect or reject the call (for example, checking context.ModelState.IsValid and setting context.Result to a BadRequestObjectResult to short-circuit invalid input before it ever reaches your action code); OnActionExecuted runs immediately after, letting you inspect the outcome or any exception via context.Exception. Exception filters activate only when an unhandled exception escapes the action, giving centralized MVC-level error handling. Result filters wrap the execution of the action's result (like rendering a view or serializing to JSON), letting you modify headers or content right before/after the response is actually written. You implement an action filter by inheriting ActionFilterAttribute, applying it as an attribute on an action or controller, or registering it globally via builder.Services.AddControllers(o => o.Filters.Add<T>()) so it runs for every action.

codeExample.explanation: LogActionFilter short-circuits invalid ModelState with a 400 before the action runs, and logs any exception the action threw afterward — both impossible from plain middleware, which has no concept of ModelState.

mistakes: Confusing filters with middleware and putting HTTP-wide concerns (like static file serving) into a filter, where they'd never apply to non-MVC requests.
Forgetting that Exception filters only catch exceptions thrown inside the MVC action pipeline, not ones thrown by middleware earlier in the request.
Not checking ModelState.IsValid in an action filter or the action itself, letting invalid input reach business logic.
Overriding the wrong method (e.g. OnResultExecuting instead of OnActionExecuting) and being confused when the filter runs at the wrong stage.
Applying an expensive filter globally when it's only needed on a handful of actions, adding overhead to every request.

followUps.question: Filter vs Middleware — what's the real difference?
followUps.answer: Middleware is HTTP-level, runs for every request regardless of whether MVC handles it, and knows nothing about controllers or ModelState. Filters run inside the MVC pipeline and can see the action, its arguments, ModelState, and the result. Rule of thumb: need MVC context → filter; need it on all traffic including static files → middleware.

followUps.question: Which filter type would you use for centralized error handling, and are there better alternatives?
followUps.answer: An Exception filter, implementing IExceptionFilter, is the MVC-native option, but it only catches exceptions inside the MVC pipeline — it misses errors thrown by middleware earlier in the request. For truly global handling, exception-handling middleware (registered first in the pipeline) or the modern IExceptionHandler with AddExceptionHandler is usually preferred.

followUps.question: Can you short-circuit the pipeline from an action filter?
followUps.answer: Yes — setting context.Result inside OnActionExecuting (an ActionExecutingContext) prevents the action method from running at all and returns that result instead, which is exactly how a global ModelState validation filter works.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Filters are TV studio crew stations — each one only activates at its own stage of the broadcast.
memoryHack.mnemonic: AR-A-E-R: AuthZ, Resource, Action, Exception, Result.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Walk the TV studio: security guard at the door (Authorization), stage manager's prop check (Resource), floor director yelling rolling/cut around the live take (Action), the emergency crew only if a camera catches fire (Exception), and the broadcast engineer tweaking output right before air (Result).

bestPractices: Use a global ModelState-validation action filter instead of repeating if (!ModelState.IsValid) checks in every action.
Prefer middleware over filters for concerns that must apply to all HTTP traffic, not just MVC-routed requests.
Keep filters focused on one cross-cutting concern (logging, validation, caching) for reuse across controllers.
Register filters globally only when truly needed everywhere; otherwise scope them to specific controllers/actions.
performanceTips: Resource filters can short-circuit before model binding runs, making them cheaper than action filters for early rejection scenarios like response caching.
Avoid heavy synchronous work inside OnActionExecuting/OnActionExecuted; prefer the async filter interfaces (IAsyncActionFilter) for I/O-bound work.

quiz.question: Which filter type runs only when an unhandled exception occurs?
quiz.explanation: Exception filters activate specifically when an unhandled exception escapes an action, for centralized MVC-level error handling.

quiz.question: What can you access in a filter that you cannot in plain middleware?
quiz.explanation: Filters run inside the MVC pipeline and have access to MVC-specific context like ModelState and the action's arguments, which middleware has no concept of.

flashcards.front: What are the five filter types in order?
flashcards.back: Authorization, Resource, Action, Exception, Result.

flashcards.front: What does OnActionExecuting let you do?
flashcards.back: Run code (and optionally short-circuit via context.Result) before the action executes.

flashcards.front: Filter vs middleware — key distinction?
flashcards.back: Filters run inside MVC with action context; middleware is HTTP-level and applies to all requests.

flashcards.front: How do you register a filter globally?
flashcards.back: builder.Services.AddControllers(o => o.Filters.Add<T>()).

revision30: Filters run at specific MVC pipeline stages — Authorization, Resource, Action, Exception, Result — and unlike middleware, have access to action context like ModelState. Action filters use OnActionExecuting/OnActionExecuted around the action call.
revision2min: Filters are MVC-pipeline-specific checkpoints for concerns that need action-level context. Authorization filters run first, backing [Authorize]. Resource filters run after authorization but before model binding, useful for caching or early short-circuiting. Action filters wrap the action method itself: OnActionExecuting runs just before (and can set context.Result to short-circuit, e.g. rejecting invalid ModelState with a 400), OnActionExecuted runs just after (and can inspect context.Exception). Exception filters only fire when an unhandled exception escapes the action. Result filters wrap the execution of the action's result, letting you adjust the response right before/after it's written. You build an action filter by inheriting ActionFilterAttribute and applying it as an attribute, or registering it globally with builder.Services.AddControllers(o => o.Filters.Add<T>()). The key interview distinction is filter vs middleware: middleware is HTTP-level and runs for every request including static files, with no knowledge of controllers; filters run inside MVC and can see the action, its arguments, ModelState, and the result — so cross-cutting concerns needing MVC context belong in a filter, while concerns needing to apply to all HTTP traffic belong in middleware.
challenge: Write a Result filter that adds a custom X-Response-Time header measuring how long result execution (view rendering or JSON serialization) took, and explain why this couldn't be done as cleanly in an Action filter.
summary: Filters are MVC-pipeline checkpoints (Authorization, Resource, Action, Exception, Result) that, unlike middleware, have direct access to action context like ModelState and the action's result.

title: How do you handle Global Exception handling in .NET Core?
interviewQuestion: How do you implement global exception handling in ASP.NET Core?

story.setup: Imagine a building's central fire-alarm and sprinkler system, wired to cover every single floor — not one hand-held extinguisher per office.
scenes: The sprinkler system's control panel is installed on floor zero, wired to blanket every floor above it — that's exception middleware registered FIRST in Program.cs, wrapping everything downstream.

When a fire breaks out on any floor (an unhandled exception anywhere in the pipeline), the sprinkler doesn't just spray water blindly — it checks what kind of fire it is: an electrical fire (KeyNotFoundException → 404), a chemical fire (UnauthorizedAccessException → 401), a grease fire (ValidationException → 400) — and responds with the matching status code.

The fire department's incident report (logging) is filed with full detail — exact floor, cause, time — but the announcement broadcast to tenants (the JSON response) only ever says 'a fire occurred, here's your incident number' — never the messy internal cause. That's why you log full detail server-side but return a safe message plus a traceId.

A junior building manager once tried putting the sprinkler system on the top floor only (an IExceptionFilter, which is MVC-only) — but fires that started in the elevator shafts (middleware-level errors) never triggered it, because it was scoped too narrowly.
story.moral: Global exception handling has to sit at the very top of the pipeline to catch everything beneath it, log full detail privately, and expose only a safe, correlated response to the caller.

analogy: Global exception handling is a building-wide sprinkler system wired to the top of the pipeline — it catches fires from any floor, logs the real cause internally, but only ever announces a safe incident number to tenants.
explanation: The recommended approach for global exception handling in ASP.NET Core is exception-handling middleware registered first in the pipeline, so it wraps everything downstream in a try/catch. Inside the catch block, you log the full exception detail (including a trace/correlation ID like context.TraceIdentifier) for internal diagnostics, map the exception type to the correct HTTP status code (e.g. KeyNotFoundException to 404, UnauthorizedAccessException to 401, a custom ValidationException to 400, defaulting to 500), and write a safe JSON response that never leaks stack traces or internal details, ideally including the trace ID so a user's error report can be correlated with server logs. Alternatives include app.UseExceptionHandler("/error") pointing at a dedicated error endpoint/controller, an IExceptionFilter which is MVC-only and therefore misses exceptions thrown by middleware itself, and the modern IExceptionHandler interface registered via AddExceptionHandler, which integrates cleanly with the built-in exception-handling middleware pipeline. Best practice is to return a standardized error shape, ideally RFC 7807 ProblemDetails, so API consumers get a consistent error contract.
interviewAnswerShort: Register exception-handling middleware first in the pipeline so it wraps everything, log the full exception with a trace ID server-side, map the exception type to the right HTTP status code, and return a safe ProblemDetails-style JSON response without leaking stack traces.
interviewAnswerDetailed: The most robust approach is a custom exception-handling middleware, or the built-in app.UseExceptionHandler, registered as the very first middleware in Program.cs so its try/catch wraps every other middleware and the entire MVC pipeline beneath it. Inside the catch, you log the exception with full detail — message, stack trace, and a correlation ID like context.TraceIdentifier — so you can debug from logs without exposing that detail to the client. You then map the exception's type to the appropriate HTTP status code using a switch expression: not-found scenarios to 404, authorization failures to 401, validation exceptions to 400, and anything unrecognized to a generic 500. The response body should be a safe, generic JSON object (or better, an RFC 7807 ProblemDetails payload) containing something like 'An error occurred' plus the trace ID for correlation — never the raw exception message or stack trace, which could leak internals to an attacker. Alternatives include app.UseExceptionHandler("/error") which redirects to a dedicated error-handling endpoint, an IExceptionFilter which only catches exceptions inside the MVC action pipeline (it misses anything thrown by middleware itself, including other middleware's exceptions before MVC even runs), and the newer IExceptionHandler interface registered with AddExceptionHandler, which is the modern, DI-friendly, ASP.NET Core-native pattern for this exact problem.

codeExample.explanation: Registered first, ExceptionMiddleware wraps the entire pipeline, logs full exception detail with a trace ID, maps exception types to status codes, and returns a safe generic error body.

mistakes: Registering the exception middleware anywhere but first, so earlier middleware errors escape unhandled.
Returning raw exception messages or stack traces in the JSON response, leaking internal implementation details.
Using only an IExceptionFilter and assuming it covers all exceptions, when it actually misses anything thrown by middleware.
Not including a correlation/trace ID in the error response, making it impossible to match a user's bug report to server logs.
Using try/catch for expected, normal control flow (like parsing user input) instead of TryParse-style APIs, when exceptions should be reserved for truly exceptional cases.

followUps.question: Explain try/catch/finally with the classic divide-by-zero example.
followUps.answer: try { int c = a / b; } throws DivideByZeroException for integer division; catch (DivideByZeroException ex) { } should come first since it's more specific, followed by catch (Exception ex) { throw; } as a general fallback last (or the code won't compile, since unreachable specific catches after a general one are a compile error) — throw; re-throws while preserving the original stack trace, whereas throw ex; resets it, destroying the original call site info. finally { } always runs regardless of whether an exception was thrown, which is exactly what a using block compiles down to for cleanup. Also worth noting: integer division by zero throws, but floating-point division by zero returns Infinity or NaN instead of throwing.

followUps.question: What's the difference between IExceptionFilter and exception-handling middleware?
followUps.answer: IExceptionFilter is MVC-only — it catches exceptions thrown by action execution but misses exceptions thrown by middleware itself, including middleware registered before MVC even runs. Exception-handling middleware, registered first in the pipeline, wraps everything and catches exceptions from any layer.

followUps.question: What is ProblemDetails and why use it?
followUps.answer: ProblemDetails (RFC 7807) is a standardized JSON shape for HTTP API error responses, containing fields like type, title, status, detail, and instance. Using it gives API consumers a predictable, machine-parseable error contract instead of ad hoc error shapes per endpoint.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Sprinklers on floor zero — register the exception handler first so it covers every floor above it.
memoryHack.mnemonic: LMS: Log full detail, Map to status code, Send safe response + traceId.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture the sprinkler control panel bolted to the building's foundation (registered first) — no matter which floor catches fire, it triggers, logs the real cause in the fire department's private report, and only ever tells tenants a safe incident number.

bestPractices: Always register global exception handling as the first middleware so it wraps the entire pipeline.
Log full exception detail (including stack trace and trace ID) server-side, but return only a safe, generic message to the client.
Return a standardized error shape like RFC 7807 ProblemDetails for consistent API error contracts.
Map known exception types to specific HTTP status codes rather than always returning a generic 500.
Prefer 'throw;' over 'throw ex;' when re-throwing, to preserve the original stack trace for diagnostics.
performanceTips: Exceptions are relatively expensive in .NET (stack unwinding, stack trace capture) — don't use them for expected/normal control flow like input validation; use TryParse-style patterns instead.
Keep the try block in exception middleware as small as just await _next(context) so you're not adding unnecessary overhead to every request's happy path.

quiz.question: Where should global exception-handling middleware be registered in the pipeline?
quiz.explanation: Registering it first ensures its try/catch wraps every other middleware and the entire MVC pipeline, catching exceptions from any layer.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between 'throw;' and 'throw ex;' when re-throwing?
options: throw; preserves the original stack trace; throw ex; resets it
throw; only works in finally blocks
quiz.explanation: 'throw;' re-throws the current exception preserving its original stack trace, while 'throw ex;' resets the stack trace to the current line, losing the original failure location.

flashcards.front: Where should exception middleware be registered?
flashcards.back: First in the pipeline, so it wraps everything downstream.

flashcards.front: What should the client-facing error response contain?
flashcards.back: A safe generic message plus a trace/correlation ID — never a stack trace.

flashcards.front: IExceptionFilter vs middleware for exceptions?
flashcards.back: IExceptionFilter only catches MVC action exceptions; middleware catches exceptions from any layer.

flashcards.front: throw; vs throw ex;?

title: What is a Minimal API and when would you use it over controllers?
interviewQuestion: What is a Minimal API in ASP.NET Core, and when would you use it instead of controllers?

story.setup: Compare a food truck to a full sit-down restaurant — both serve the same cuisine, but they're built for different scales.
scenes: The food truck (Minimal API) has a tiny, direct menu board bolted right to the window — app.MapGet("/orders", ...) — no host, no separate kitchen department, just a straight line from order to food.

The sit-down restaurant (Controllers) has a full org chart: hosts (routing conventions), a maître d' (model binding), specialized stations (filters), and printed multi-page menus — more ceremony, but it scales to banquet-sized events without becoming chaos.
Both kitchens use the exact same supply chain (DI) — parameters like AppDbContext or IOrderService are resolved from the container the same way whether you're a truck or a restaurant.

A startup opens five food trucks around the city instead of one giant restaurant — that's microservices: many small, focused Minimal API services, each dead simple, easier to deploy and scale independently.

A hotel chain running one massive banquet hall needs the full restaurant's structure — many menus (endpoints), consistent service standards (model validation conventions) — which is exactly when Controllers' extra ceremony pays for itself.
story.moral: Minimal APIs trade ceremony for directness — perfect for small, focused services; Controllers trade some directness for structure that scales to large, complex APIs.

analogy: A Minimal API is a food truck — a short, direct line from order to food; Controllers are a full restaurant with hosts, stations, and menus that scale to banquet-sized complexity.
explanation: Minimal APIs let you define HTTP endpoints directly in Program.cs using app.MapGet, app.MapPost, etc., without controller classes or attribute routing ceremony. Handlers are typically lambdas whose parameters — like a DbContext, a DTO, or a service interface — are resolved from the same dependency injection container as controllers, so DI behaves identically. Route-specific behaviors like authorization and endpoint naming are chained fluently, e.g. .RequireAuthorization().WithName("CreateOrder"). Minimal APIs have less boilerplate and slightly faster startup/throughput, but offer more limited filter and model-binding-convention support (endpoint filters instead of the full MVC filter pipeline) and require more manual discipline to stay organized at scale (typically by grouping endpoints into extension methods or route groups). Controllers carry more ceremony but give you the full MVC pipeline — action filters, model binding conventions, and a structure that's natural for large applications with many endpoints. Minimal APIs suit microservices, small focused services, serverless/Azure Functions-style endpoints, prototypes, and internal tooling; Controllers suit large applications with many endpoints, heavy use of filters/validation conventions, and teams that benefit from familiar, established structure.
interviewAnswerShort: Minimal APIs define endpoints directly in Program.cs with app.MapGet/MapPost lambdas instead of controller classes — less boilerplate and slightly faster, best for small services and microservices, while Controllers give you the full MVC pipeline and scale better for large, complex APIs.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Minimal APIs let you skip controller classes entirely and register endpoints directly against the WebApplication instance, e.g. app.MapGet("/orders/{id:int}", async (int id, AppDbContext db) => ...). The lambda's parameters are resolved from DI exactly the same way controller constructor parameters are, so services, DbContext, and DTOs all work identically. You can chain fluent configuration onto the mapped endpoint, like .RequireAuthorization() for auth requirements or .WithName(...) for link generation and OpenAPI metadata. Compared to controllers, Minimal APIs have dramatically less boilerplate, and benchmark slightly faster in startup time and raw throughput because there's less pipeline machinery involved. The trade-off is that Minimal APIs use endpoint filters rather than the full MVC filter pipeline (so Action/Result filters as you'd write for controllers don't directly apply), and organizing dozens of endpoints requires deliberate discipline — usually grouping related endpoints into extension methods or MapGroup route groups — whereas controllers give you that organizational structure for free through classes. In practice, Minimal APIs are the right choice for microservices, small focused services, serverless-style functions, prototypes, and internal tooling; Controllers remain the better choice for large applications with many endpoints, heavy reliance on the full MVC filter/validation pipeline, and teams who benefit from the conventional controller structure.

codeExample.explanation: Endpoints are mapped directly in Program.cs; handler parameters (AppDbContext, IOrderService, DTOs) are resolved from DI the same way as in controllers, and .RequireAuthorization() applies auth declaratively.

mistakes: Assuming Minimal APIs skip dependency injection entirely — they use the exact same DI container as controllers.
Using Minimal APIs for a large, complex API without adopting route groups or extension-method organization, leading to an unmaintainable Program.cs.
Expecting the full MVC filter pipeline (Action/Result filters) to work unmodified in Minimal APIs — they use endpoint filters instead.
Believing Minimal APIs are strictly 'worse' or 'toy-only' rather than a legitimate, production-grade option for the right scale of service.
Forgetting to chain .RequireAuthorization() on endpoints that need auth, since Minimal APIs don't get controller-level [Authorize] by default.

followUps.question: Does dependency injection work differently in Minimal APIs?
followUps.answer: No — DI works the same way. Handler lambda parameters that match a registered service type (like AppDbContext or IOrderService) are resolved from the same container used for controllers.

followUps.question: How do you keep a large Minimal API organized?
followUps.answer: Group related endpoints using MapGroup, or split endpoint registration into extension methods per feature (e.g. app.MapOrderEndpoints()), rather than letting Program.cs grow into a single massive file.

followUps.question: What do you lose by choosing Minimal APIs over Controllers?
followUps.answer: The full MVC filter pipeline (Action, Result, Resource, Exception filters as controller attributes) — Minimal APIs use a separate, more limited endpoint filter mechanism — along with the built-in model binding conventions and structure controllers provide for large teams.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Food truck (Minimal API) vs full restaurant (Controllers) — same ingredients (DI), different scale of ceremony.
